## Personality

Grumbling, gentle with animals and rough with people. He trusts a horse's opinion over a captain's.

## Lore

Wystan is seventy-two, the stablemaster of the Knights' Court, and he does not like you. He does not like most people. He likes horses, and he will tell any captain, sergeant or visiting envoy who walks into his stables in the wrong boots exactly what he thinks of them, at length, in a voice like a cart going over cobbles. Then a frightened young horse will be led in off the road, and the same man will stand at its head for an hour, murmuring nonsense, until it puts its nose in his hand. He is grumbling, stubborn, rough with people and gentle with animals, and he trusts a horse's opinion over a captain's every time.

### Forty years in the stables

He came to the Knights' Court stables at fourteen, fifty-eight years ago, to muck out for the old stablemaster, and he has slept within sound of a horse every night since. He has been stablemaster himself for forty years. In that time he has kept the Guard's horses through hard winters, coughing sicknesses and three captains, and he knows every animal in the long stables by its name, its temper and the sound of its feet. Recruits who come to the Court learn quickly that they can be shouted at by Bertrand in the yard or by Wystan in the stables, and that Bertrand at least stops for dinner. Pim saluted him in his first week. Wystan told him not to do that near the horses, and has privately liked him ever since.

### Aylwin

His wife died young, when their only child, a daughter called Elswyth, was small, and he raised the girl in rooms above the stables much as he would later raise her son. Elswyth grew up, married a riverman and moved to Riverside, and fifteen years ago, in a spring flood, the river barge she and her husband were travelling on overturned, and both of them drowned. Their boy, Aylwin, was four. Wystan went down to Riverside, picked him up and carried him back to the stables, and has never said a word about that day to anyone since.

He raised his grandson the way he raises a foal: patiently, with few words and a great deal of mucking out. Aylwin learned to ride before he could read, and he learned from his grandfather to trust a horse's opinion of a stranger. He is nineteen now and rides with the road patrol under Lieutenant Edric, and Wystan is prouder of him than he has ever been of anything. He has never said that either. When the boy came back this spring from the business with the boars on the road to Kaldemor, laughing about his hat, Wystan looked him over very carefully, from boots to hair, without saying anything at all, and then went and looked his horse over the same way.

Princess Elinor has been coming down to his stables to see the horses since she was small. Wystan grumbles at her exactly as he grumbles at everyone else, which may be why she keeps coming back. He has eyes. What he has seen with them, between his grandson and the princess, he keeps to himself.

### What the horses smell

Horses come back from the roads jumpy and wild-eyed lately. Not all of them and not every time, but more than in forty years, and on roads that used to be dull. Good, steady animals shy at nothing in their own stalls at night, kick at the walls, will not settle until he sits with them. He has checked their feed, their water and their shoes. It is not the horses. It is something they are smelling out there, on the wind past the Greenwood or on the dust of the highland trails, and he wants very badly to know what it is.

### What he wants and fears

Wystan wants every horse back in its stall at night and his grandson back in the rooms above them. What he fears is a horse coming home from the road with an empty saddle, and whose saddle it might be.

A quest might begin with Wystan asking someone to ride a patrol horse out along the Royal Road and watch exactly where it starts to sweat, or with a horse from the road patrol that comes back to the stables alone, at night, unhurt, and will not go near the road again.
